content: Database migration projects with more than 100 tables should never attempt a big-bang cutover. Use phased migration: migrate schema-by-schema or function-by-function, with reconciliation at each phase. The migration tool (Liquibase, Flyway, custom) must support rollback per phase.

Real-time sync between two systems is architecturally 10x harder than batch sync. Before committing to real-time, ask: Is batch (hourly/daily) actually sufficient? What's the business cost of 1-hour latency? If real-time is truly needed, use event-driven architecture (Kafka, Pub/Sub) with idempotent consumers and a dead-letter queue.

450+ table sync between heterogeneous databases is not a tool problem — it's an architecture problem. Pattern: CDC (Change Data Capture) from source → transformation layer → destination. Tools: Debezium for CDC, Kafka Connect for transport, custom transforms for schema mapping. Never try to sync application-to-application.

Microservices migration from a monolith should follow the Strangler Fig pattern: new functionality goes into services, existing functionality is extracted incrementally. Never rewrite from scratch. The monolith stays live until all traffic is routed through the new services. Budget 2-3 years for a serious decomposition.

For any system replacement, the critical question is: what custom business logic exists in the old system that isn't documented? This is the #1 surprise in migrations. Discovery method: run a code audit looking for stored procedures, triggers, scheduled jobs, and hardcoded business rules. Budget 20% of migration effort for undocumented logic discovery.

API-first architecture is the safest integration pattern. Define OpenAPI specs before implementation, use contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract), version all APIs, and implement backwards-compatible changes only. Breaking changes require a new version and a deprecation period.

For high-availability requirements (99.9%+), the architecture must be active-active across at least two availability zones. This doubles infrastructure cost but eliminates single-region failure. Ask the client: Is the cost of downtime greater than the cost of active-active? Most enterprise clients underestimate downtime cost.

Data lake vs data warehouse is not either/or. Pattern: raw data lands in the data lake (cheap storage, schema-on-read), then curated datasets are loaded into the data warehouse (structured, schema-on-write, fast queries). The lake is the source of truth; the warehouse is the serving layer.

For greenfield projects, start with a monolith and extract services only when there's a clear need (team scaling, independent deployability, different scaling requirements). Premature microservices add 3-5x operational complexity with no benefit until the team and scale justify it.

Event sourcing is powerful but complex. Use it only when: audit trail is a hard requirement, temporal queries (state at time T) are needed, or event replay is valuable. For most CRUD applications, traditional state-based persistence is simpler and sufficient. Event sourcing adds 2-3x development effort.
